topicName: Periodic Table Trends and Element Positions
description: Covers how elements are arranged into groups and periods, how electron configuration determines an element's position, and the trends in metallic character and reactivity across periods and down groups.

mcq.questionText: In the periodic table, the vertical columns are called groups and the horizontal rows are called:
mcq.explanation: Vertical = groups; horizontal = periods. Exam Tip: Groups go down; periods go across.

mcq.questionText: Elements in the same group of the periodic table have the same number of:
mcq.explanation: Same group members have the same number of outer-shell electrons. Exam Tip: Same group -> same valence electrons -> similar chemical properties.

mcq.questionText: The period number of an element tells us the number of:
mcq.explanation: The period number equals the number of occupied electron shells. Exam Tip: Period number = number of shells. Group number = number of outer electrons.

mcq.questionText: An element with the electronic configuration 2, 8, 1 belongs to Group:
mcq.explanation: The group number equals the outer-shell electrons: the outer shell has 1 electron. Exam Tip: Outer electrons = group number. This element (2,8,1) is sodium, Group 1.

mcq.questionText: An element with the electronic configuration 2, 8, 1 is in Period:
mcq.explanation: The period number equals the number of shells used: 2,8,1 uses three shells. Exam Tip: Count the shells (numbers in the configuration): three numbers = Period 3.

mcq.questionText: Group 1 elements (such as sodium and potassium) are known as the:
mcq.explanation: They are the alkali metals. Exam Tip: Group 1 = alkali metals. Group 7 = halogens. Group 8/0 = noble gases.

mcq.questionText: Group 8 (0) elements, such as helium and argon, are called the noble gases because they are:

options.text: Unreactive (inert) due to full outer shells

mcq.explanation: They have full outer shells, so they are stable and unreactive. Exam Tip: Noble gases have full outer shells -> very stable -> unreactive.

mcq.questionText: Across a period, from left to right, the metallic character of elements generally:
mcq.explanation: Metals are on the left, non-metals on the right - metallic character decreases across. Exam Tip: Across a period (left to right): metallic character decreases.

mcq.questionText: Down a group, the metallic character of elements generally:
mcq.explanation: Elements become more metallic (more reactive metals) going down. Exam Tip: Down a group, metallic character INCREASES.

mcq.questionText: Elements in Group 7, such as chlorine and fluorine, are called the:
mcq.explanation: They are the halogens. Exam Tip: Group 7 = halogens (reactive non-metals, 7 outer electrons).

mcq.questionText: An element with 7 electrons in its outer shell is most likely to:

options.text: Gain 1 electron to complete its outer shell

mcq.explanation: 7 outer electrons need just 1 more; gaining 1 is easier than losing 7. Exam Tip: Near-full outer shells (6, 7 electrons) GAIN electrons -> non-metals.

mcq.questionText: Which element is the most reactive metal in Group 1 among lithium, sodium and potassium?
mcq.explanation: Reactivity of Group 1 metals increases down the group, so potassium, being lowest of the three, is the most reactive. Exam Tip: Down Group 1, reactivity INCREASES (Li < Na < K).

mcq.questionText: Elements are classified as metals or non-metals depending mainly on their:

options.text: Number of outer-shell electrons and their properties

mcq.explanation: Few outer electrons -> metal (lose electrons); many -> non-metal (gain electrons). Exam Tip: Few outer electrons (1-3) -> metals. Many (5-7) -> non-metals.

mcq.questionText: An element X has the configuration 2, 8, 8. Which family does it belong to?
mcq.explanation: Full outer shell of 8 means a stable, unreactive element. Exam Tip: Full outer shell (8) -> noble gas (here argon, 2,8,8).

mcq.questionText: Two elements in the same group of the periodic table are expected to have:
mcq.explanation: Same group means the same number of valence electrons -> similar chemical behaviour. Exam Tip: Group members react similarly because reactions depend on outer (valence) electrons.

fib.questionText: The horizontal rows of the periodic table are called ____.
fib.explanation: Periods are the horizontal rows of the periodic table, while groups are the vertical columns. Exam Tip: Periods = rows; groups = columns.

fib.questionText: Elements in the same ____ have the same number of outer-shell electrons.
fib.explanation: Elements in the same group share the same number of valence electrons, giving them similar properties. Exam Tip: Same group -> similar properties.

fib.questionText: The period number of an element equals the number of ____ it has.
fib.explanation: The period number tells you how many electron shells (energy levels) an atom uses. Exam Tip: Count the shells to get the period.

fib.questionText: Group 1 elements are called the ____ metals.
fib.explanation: Group 1 elements such as lithium, sodium and potassium are known as alkali metals. Exam Tip: Alkali metals (Li, Na, K) are very reactive.

fib.questionText: Group 8 (0) elements are called the ____ gases because they are unreactive.
fib.explanation: Group 8 (0) elements are called noble gases because their full outer shells make them stable and unreactive. Exam Tip: Noble gases have full outer shells -> inert.

fib.questionText: Across a period from left to right, the non-metallic character of elements generally ____.
fib.explanation: Moving left to right across a period, elements gain more outer electrons and become more non-metallic. Exam Tip: Across: non-metallic up, metallic down.

fib.questionText: Down a group, the reactivity of the alkali metals (Group 1) ____.
fib.explanation: Down Group 1, the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more easily lost, so reactivity increases. Exam Tip: Li < Na < K in reactivity.

fib.questionText: An element with 1 electron in its outer shell is likely to be a ____ (metal/non-metal).
fib.explanation: One outer electron is easily lost, so the element behaves as a reactive metal. Exam Tip: 1 outer electron -> very reactive metal (Group 1).

fib.questionText: Group 7 elements are known as the ____.
fib.explanation: Group 7 elements such as fluorine and chlorine are known as the halogens. Exam Tip: Halogens (F, Cl, Br) are reactive non-metals.

fib.questionText: An element with a full outer shell of electrons is ____ (reactive/unreactive).
fib.explanation: A full outer shell gives an atom a stable electron arrangement, so it does not readily react. Exam Tip: Full outer shell = noble gas = unreactive.

tf.questionText: Elements in the same group have the same number of outer-shell electrons.
tf.explanation: This is why group members react similarly, since chemical behaviour depends on outer-shell (valence) electrons. Exam Tip: This is why group members react similarly.

tf.questionText: The period number of an element equals the number of protons it has.
tf.explanation: The period number equals the number of electron shells, not the number of protons; the number of protons is the atomic number. Exam Tip: Period = shells; atomic number = protons.

tf.questionText: Group 1 elements are called the alkali metals.
tf.explanation: Group 1 elements such as lithium, sodium and potassium are indeed known as alkali metals. Exam Tip: Alkali metals are very reactive and stored under oil.

tf.questionText: Metallic character increases across a period from left to right.
tf.explanation: Metallic character actually decreases from left to right across a period as elements become more non-metallic. Exam Tip: Metallic character DECREASES from left to right.

tf.questionText: Noble gases are unreactive because they have full outer electron shells.
tf.explanation: A full outer shell gives noble gases a stable electron arrangement, making them chemically unreactive. Exam Tip: Full outer shell = stability.

tf.questionText: Reactivity of Group 1 metals decreases down the group.
tf.explanation: Reactivity of Group 1 metals actually increases down the group as the outer electron becomes easier to lose. Exam Tip: Group 1 reactivity INCREASES down the group.

tf.questionText: An element with 7 outer electrons is likely to gain 1 electron to become stable.
tf.explanation: An atom with 7 outer electrons needs just 1 more to complete its outer shell, so it readily gains an electron. Exam Tip: Near-full shells gain electrons -> non-metals (halogens).

tf.questionText: Group 7 elements are called noble gases.
tf.explanation: Group 7 elements are called halogens; noble gases belong to Group 8 (0). Exam Tip: Group 7 = halogens; noble gases are Group 8 (0).

tf.questionText: The number of outer-shell electrons equals the group number for main-group elements.
tf.explanation: For main-group elements, the number of electrons in the outer shell directly gives the group number. Exam Tip: 2,8,1 -> 1 outer electron -> Group 1.

tf.questionText: Elements in the same group have similar chemical properties.
tf.explanation: Chemical behaviour depends mainly on the outer electrons, which are the same for elements within a group. Exam Tip: Chemical behaviour depends on the outer electrons, which are the same within a group.

summary.correctAnswer: Groups are the vertical columns of the periodic table; periods are the horizontal rows.
summary.explanation: Elements in a group share chemical properties, while elements in a period show trends across the table. Exam Tip: Groups go down (columns), periods go across (rows).

summary.correctAnswer: For main-group elements, the group number equals the number of electrons in the outer (valence) shell.
summary.explanation: For example, an element with configuration 2,8,1 has 1 outer electron and belongs to Group 1. Exam Tip: Outer electrons = group number.

summary.correctAnswer: The period number equals the number of electron shells (energy levels) occupied by an atom.
summary.explanation: For example, the configuration 2,8,1 uses three shells, so the element is in Period 3. Exam Tip: Count the numbers in the electron configuration to find the period.

summary.correctAnswer: The Group 1 elements, such as lithium, sodium and potassium, which are very reactive metals with 1 outer electron.
summary.explanation: Alkali metals become more reactive down the group and are stored under oil because they react vigorously with water and air. Exam Tip: Group 1 = alkali metals; reactivity increases down the group.

summary.correctAnswer: The Group 8 (0) elements, such as helium, neon and argon, which have full outer shells and are chemically unreactive.
summary.explanation: Their stable, full outer shells mean noble gases rarely form compounds. Exam Tip: Full outer shell -> noble gas -> unreactive.

summary.correctAnswer: The Group 7 elements, such as fluorine, chlorine and bromine, which are reactive non-metals with 7 outer electrons.
summary.explanation: Halogens readily gain 1 electron to complete their outer shell and become stable. Exam Tip: Group 7 = halogens = 7 outer electrons, gain 1 to react.

summary.questionText: Metallic character trend across a period
summary.correctAnswer: Metallic character decreases from left to right across a period as elements become more non-metallic.
summary.explanation: Metals sit on the left of a period and non-metals on the right, so properties shift from metallic to non-metallic. Exam Tip: Across a period (left to right): metallic character decreases.

summary.questionText: Metallic character trend down a group
summary.correctAnswer: Metallic character increases down a group as atoms become larger and outer electrons are held less strongly.
summary.explanation: This is why elements lower in a group, such as potassium compared to lithium, behave more like typical reactive metals. Exam Tip: Down a group: metallic character increases.

summary.correctAnswer: Reactivity of the alkali metals increases down Group 1, from lithium to sodium to potassium.
summary.explanation: Going down the group, the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more easily lost, making reactions with water more vigorous. Exam Tip: Li < Na < K in reactivity.

summary.questionText: Metal vs non-metal by outer electrons
summary.correctAnswer: Elements with few outer-shell electrons (1-3) tend to be metals that lose electrons, while elements with many outer-shell electrons (5-7) tend to be non-metals that gain electrons.
summary.explanation: An element with a full outer shell (8 electrons) is a stable, unreactive noble gas. Exam Tip: Few outer electrons -> metal; many outer electrons -> non-metal; full outer shell -> noble gas.

hoq.questionText: An element Q has the electronic configuration 2, 8, 2. Determine its group and period, and predict whether it is a metal or non-metal.
hoq.explanation: Last shell has 2 -> Group 2. Three shells (2,8,2) -> Period 3. Only 2 outer electrons -> lost easily -> metal. Exam Tip: LAST number = group; COUNT of numbers = period. Few outer electrons (1-3) -> metal. This is magnesium.

hoq.questionText: Three elements: X (2,8,1), Y (2,8,7), Z (2,8,8). Predict how each behaves in reactions and identify which is unreactive.

options.text: X loses 1 electron (metal); Y gains 1 electron (non-metal); Z is unreactive (full shell)
X gains electrons; Y loses electrons; Z is a metal

hoq.explanation: X (1 outer electron) loses it - reactive metal. Y (7 outer electrons) gains 1 - reactive non-metal. Z (full shell of 8) - stable, unreactive. Exam Tip: 1 electron -> lose (metal); 7 electrons -> gain (non-metal); 8 electrons (full) -> unreactive (noble gas).

hoq.questionText: Going DOWN Group 1 (Li -> Na -> K), the metals react more vigorously with water. Explain this trend using the outer electron.

options.text: The outer electron gets closer to the nucleus, so reactivity falls
Going down the group, the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more easily lost, so reactivity increases
The metals gain electrons more easily going down
All Group 1 metals react the same

hoq.explanation: Group 1 metals react by losing their single outer electron. Down the group, atoms are larger, the outer electron is further from the nucleus and less strongly held, so it is lost more easily. Exam Tip: For metals, easier loss of the outer electron = greater reactivity. This is why potassium reacts far more violently with water than lithium.
